articles.title: Breathing less oxygen tripled lifespan in mice with a deadly brain disorder
articles.summary: Oxygen is essential for life, but too much of it can become dangerously toxic, particularly in people with certain neurological and mitochondrial disorders. Scientists at Gladstone Institutes have discovered that defective proteins can disrupt the ability of mitochondria to consume oxygen, allowing harmful levels to accumulate in tissues. Remarkably, mice with a genetic disorder that causes motor neuron degeneration lived three times longer when they breathed air containing less oxygen.
articles.content:
Oxygen is essential for human survival and for most forms of life. Yet under certain conditions, it can become dangerously toxic, causing serious damage to the body.

In the brain, excessive oxygen levels have been linked to a rare and often fatal childhood disorder called 3-MGA, as well as Leigh syndrome (the most common pediatric mitochondrial disease), Parkinson's disease, and premature aging. Researchers at Gladstone Institutes are now investigating a promising approach that could potentially help treat these conditions by reducing the amount of oxygen available to the body, a strategy known as hypoxia therapy.

For the past decade, Gladstone Investigator Isha Jain, PhD, has studied how oxygen levels influence health and disease. Her research has explored how the reduced oxygen availability at high altitudes can produce beneficial effects in conditions ranging from Leigh syndrome and diabetes to solid tumors.

Expanding the Potential of Hypoxia Therapy

Jain and her colleagues wanted to determine whether lowering oxygen levels could also benefit people with other rare and common conditions involving mitochondrial dysfunction and neurological damage.

For a new study published in Nature Metabolism, the team partnered with James Shorter, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biophysics at the University of Pennsylvania, and Daniel Southworth, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biophysics at UC San Francisco.

The researchers discovered that a malfunctioning protein known as HTRA2 can cause oxygen to accumulate to dangerous levels in tissues. Remarkably, reducing the oxygen concentration in the air dramatically extended lifespan and improved brain function in mice experiencing motor neuron degeneration caused by defective HTRA2.

"This protein is linked to many other conditions, so our findings suggest that hypoxia therapy could be transformative for treating many neurological diseases," says Jain, who is also a core investigator at Arc Institute.

How Excess Oxygen Becomes Toxic to the Brain

Most cells contain tiny structures called mitochondria, which use oxygen to generate the energy the body needs to function. One of the most important components of this energy production system is Complex 1, the largest molecular machine within the mitochondria's respiratory machinery.

"Every time we breathe, 90 percent of the oxygen we consume goes to our mitochondria," says Ankur Garg, PhD, postdoctoral fellow in Jain's lab and first author of the study. "But if Complex 1 malfunctions, the mitochondria can no longer burn off oxygen at normal rates."

When mitochondria lose their ability to consume oxygen efficiently, the unused oxygen can accumulate in surrounding tissues and eventually reach toxic levels. This process can contribute to the brain damage associated with certain mitochondrial and neurological disorders. The researchers suspected that reducing oxygen availability might help prevent some of this damage.

Identifying Genetic Causes of Oxygen Toxicity

To identify diseases that might respond to hypoxia therapy, the team revisited data from an earlier large experiment. They searched for genes whose absence impaired cell growth under normal oxygen conditions but allowed cells to grow normally when oxygen levels were reduced.

By comparing these results with a database of known genetic disorders, the researchers identified 75 genes directly associated with diseases that could potentially benefit from hypoxia therapy.

Among the most promising candidates was the gene encoding HTRA2. Further investigation revealed that HTRA2 works alongside another protein (CLPB) to maintain the structural integrity of Complex 1.

"Together, these two proteins act like a clean-up crew inside mitochondria, preventing the machinery from becoming clogged with clumps of misfolded proteins," says Jain.

The team found that when HTRA2 and CLPB are absent or malfunctioning, this cellular maintenance system breaks down. As a result, a critical component of Complex 1 stops functioning properly.

Breathing Less Oxygen Triples Lifespan in Mice

To determine whether reducing oxygen levels could provide therapeutic benefits in a living organism, the researchers conducted experiments on mice deficient in HTRA2.

Mice that breathed air containing less oxygen lived three times as long as those breathing normal atmospheric air, which contains approximately 21 percent oxygen. The treatment also reduced inflammation in the striatum, a region of the brain.

"By showing these mice could be successfully treated with low oxygen, our study expands the potential of hypoxia therapy to a wide range of conditions that affect mitochondrial Complex 1, either directly or indirectly as in the case of HTRA2 deficiency," Garg says. "This will motivate a broader application of 'turning the oxygen dial' to conditions ranging from rare genetic diseases to common neurological conditions and beyond."

Developing a Drug That Mimics Low Oxygen

Although the experiments involved having mice breathe air with reduced oxygen concentrations, Jain and her colleagues are working toward a more practical approach. They are developing a drug called HypoxyStat that could potentially reproduce the therapeutic benefits of low oxygen through a pill or injection.

"Right now, no treatments are uniformly available for mitochondrial diseases, and hypoxia therapy offers the hope that we could treat not just one, but many of these genetic conditions," Jain says. "We're working hard to make it a practical treatment for human patients in the clinic."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough where reducing oxygen levels tripled lifespan in mice with a deadly brain disorder linked to mitochondrial dysfunction. This discovery has broad implications for treating rare and common neurological diseases, offering hope for new therapies. The study is detailed and focuses on a single, impactful topic with potential large-scale benefits for patients with mitochondrial and neurological disorders.

articles.title: Chromosome ‘glue’ could boost fertility by stabilizing ageing eggs
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 26 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03874-7A system tested in mice mimics a protein that declines with age and could help to improve fertility treatments in future.
articles.content:
Chromosomes are held together with protein structures called cohesins, but these diminish with age.Credit: Power and Syred/Science Photo Library

Researchers have engineered a ‘molecular glue’ that can stabilize chromosomes in ageing mouse eggs1. They say their artificial cohesion system could pave the way for improved fertility treatments for women over the age of 35.

Chromosomes in animal eggs are held together by protein structures called cohesins. These help to ensure that chromosomes divide correctly during the process of cell division. But the level of cohesins declines as women age, which can cause chromosomes to separate early and be distributed incorrectly. The resulting eggs can have too many or too few chromosomes, a condition known as aneuploidy, which is a cause of infertility, failed in-vitro-fertilization (IVF) treatments and early pregnancy loss, particularly in women who are more than 35 years old.

To prevent this premature separation of chromosomes in eggs, Melina Schuh, a biochemist at Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences in Göttingen, Germany, and her colleagues designed an artificial system called TALhesin. The system uses engineered proteins that attach to regions of the chromosome in which cohesin is usually present, these proteins then bind to one another.

Many groups are trying to understand cohesin because it diminishes as women age, affecting fertility, says Bettina Mihalas, a reproductive biologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, but this is the first approach to replace the protein’s function with an engineered system. “It’s a very creative, well-engineered and well-thought-out approach,” she says.

The findings were published in Science1 on 26 November.

Genetic instructions

The researchers injected messenger RNA that encoded the engineered proteins into immature mouse eggs. The mouse eggs then produced the proteins. Using fluorescence microscopy imaging, the researchers confirmed that the TALhesin proteins attached to chromosome regions in which natural cohesin is normally lost.

The artificial system reduced the frequency of early chromosome separation in older mice aged 13 months, 17 months and 20 months compared with untreated eggs. In 17-month-old mice, the proportion of eggs without any premature chromosome-separation errors increased from 46.7% to 74.1% in those treated with TALhesin, similar to what is observed in eggs from young mice.

Chromatids — the two identical halves formed by a replicating chromosome — must separate at the right time during cell division. To enable this, the researchers added a ‘molecular scissor’ into their artificial system. This switched off the artificial cohesion system at the appropriate time.

Human chromosomes

The team has adapted the system to deliver engineered proteins that attach to regions of human chromosomes in which cohesin is usually present.

Experiments in donated human eggs showed that the TALhesin proteins accumulated in these regions. The researchers also found that chromosomes with high levels of the engineered proteins tended to have smaller distances between chromatids. This demonstrates that the TALhesin system holds the chromosomes together.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough where researchers engineered a molecular system that stabilizes chromosomes in aging eggs, potentially improving fertility treatments for women over 35. This has broad implications for reproductive health, addressing a common cause of infertility and pregnancy loss, and includes successful testing in both mice and human eggs, indicating substantial real-world impact and meaningful scope.
articles.personality_title: New molecular glue helps keep chromosomes together in aging eggs
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – As women get older, a protein called cohesin that holds chromosomes together in eggs starts to disappear. This can cause the chromosomes to separate too early, leading to eggs with the wrong number of chromosomes. This problem often causes infertility and pregnancy loss, especially in women over 35.

**What happened** – Scientists in Germany created an artificial system called TALhesin that acts like cohesin. They tested it by injecting instructions for making TALhesin proteins into mouse eggs. These proteins stuck to the chromosomes and helped keep them together in older eggs. This reduced errors in chromosome separation in older mice. The team also tested TALhesin in human eggs and found it attached correctly and helped hold chromosomes together.

**Impact** – This is the first time researchers have made an engineered system that replaces the natural protein’s job in eggs. It could lead to better fertility treatments for women who have trouble because of aging eggs. By helping chromosomes stay together longer, TALhesin may lower the chance of eggs with the wrong chromosomes, which often cause failed pregnancies and IVF problems.

**What's next step** – The researchers will likely continue testing TALhesin to make sure it is safe and effective in human eggs. If successful, this system could be developed into treatments that improve fertility for older women.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have designed a new molecular tool that helps hold chromosomes together in aging eggs, which could improve fertility treatments for women over 35.

articles.title: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage. The molecule, already available as a dietary supplement, could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.
articles.content:
Researchers have identified a naturally occurring molecule that plays a crucial role in building muscle strength and improving physical performance. Released during exercise, the molecule could also provide the basis for future treatments to protect against muscle damage associated with type 2 diabetes.

The molecule, known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), is essential for muscles to adapt to physical activity. It helps muscles become stronger, improves their resistance to fatigue, and protects against damage and weakness.

The study, published in Nature Communications and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), reveals that L-BAIBA is a central regulator of the biological changes that allow muscles to improve their strength, structure, and endurance in response to exercise training.

How Exercise Triggers a Natural Muscle Booster

Although the health benefits of exercise are well established, scientists still do not fully understand the biological processes that allow the body to adapt to physical demands. A research team led by Professor Lee Roberts at the University of Leeds investigated whether these processes could reveal new ways to treat chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes.

L-BAIBA has attracted scientific interest for more than a decade. In research published in 2014, Roberts demonstrated that the molecule has beneficial effects on metabolism, helping to enhance the body's ability to burn fat in response to exercise. L-BAIBA is now commercially available as a dietary supplement.

The latest findings reveal another important function of the molecule. L-BAIBA acts as a chemical messenger that connects physical activity with beneficial changes in muscle structure and metabolism, helping muscles adapt to the demands placed on them.

Lee Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said: "Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance.

"This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes."

Protecting Muscles Against Damage From Type 2 Diabetes

The researchers also discovered that L-BAIBA protects muscles against damage associated with type 2 diabetes. The condition can negatively affect muscle health, leading to a decline in muscle mass and strength, as well as disruptions in the way muscles process and use energy. These complications can significantly reduce a person's quality of life.

Because regular physical activity is an important part of managing type 2 diabetes, finding ways to improve muscle function and reduce fatigue could make a substantial difference for people who struggle to exercise.

Type 2 diabetes is a serious chronic condition that increases the risk of potentially life-threatening complications, including heart attacks and strokes. Its development is influenced by a complex combination of factors, including age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity.

Although type 2 diabetes has traditionally been more common among older adults, diagnoses in people younger than 40 have been rising in recent years. Cases in this younger age group are now increasing more rapidly than among adults over 40.

A Promising Target for Future Diabetes Treatments

Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: "Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives."

Although the discovery opens promising avenues for future treatments, further research is needed to determine whether L-BAIBA supplementation can produce meaningful therapeutic benefits in people with type 2 diabetes.

The research was led by the University of Leeds in collaboration with:

Harvard Medical School, United States

University of São Paulo, Brazil

Wageningen University, Netherlands

Newcastle University, United Kingdom

The study was funded by Diabetes UK and BBSRC.

articles.personality_title: Scientists engineer plant to produce important cancer drug
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Paclitaxel is a chemotherapy drug used to treat several types of cancer. Traditionally, it is extracted from the bark of the Pacific yew tree, a process that is slow and can harm the environment.

**What happened** – Researchers have successfully modified a plant related to tobacco to produce paclitaxel. This new method was demonstrated in a recent study published in November 2026. Instead of relying on rare trees, the plant now makes the drug naturally.

**Impact** – This breakthrough could make producing paclitaxel faster, cheaper, and more sustainable. It may also help increase access to this vital medicine for cancer patients around the world, especially where drug supplies are limited.

**What’s next step** – Scientists will work on improving the amount of drug the plant produces and test how well this method can be scaled up for industrial drug manufacturing.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A tobacco-related plant has been engineered to produce the cancer drug paclitaxel, offering a new way to make this important medicine more efficiently and sustainably.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques modifient une plante pour produire un médicament anticancéreux important
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le paclitaxel est un médicament de chimiothérapie utilisé pour traiter plusieurs types de cancer. Il est traditionnellement extrait de l'écorce de l'if du Pacifique, un processus lent et qui peut nuire à l'environnement.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs ont réussi à modifier une plante apparentée au tabac pour produire du paclitaxel. Cette nouvelle méthode a été démontrée dans une étude publiée en novembre 2026. Au lieu de dépendre d'arbres rares, la plante fabrique désormais le médicament naturellement.

**Impact** – Cette avancée pourrait rendre la production de paclitaxel plus rapide, moins chère et plus durable. Elle pourrait aussi aider à augmenter l'accès à ce médicament vital pour les patients atteints de cancer dans le monde entier, surtout là où les fournitures sont limitées.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques vont améliorer la quantité de médicament produite par la plante et tester comment cette méthode peut être utilisée à grande échelle pour la fabrication industrielle.

**Phrase clé** – Une plante apparentée au tabac a été modifiée pour produire le médicament anticancéreux paclitaxel, offrant une nouvelle façon de fabriquer ce médicament important plus efficacement et durablement.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos modifican una planta para producir un medicamento importante contra el cáncer
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El paclitaxel es un medicamento de quimioterapia usado para tratar varios tipos de cáncer. Tradicionalmente, se extrae de la corteza del tejo del Pacífico, un proceso lento que puede dañar el medio ambiente.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores lograron modificar una planta relacionada con el tabaco para producir paclitaxel. Este nuevo método se mostró en un estudio publicado en noviembre de 2026. En lugar de depender de árboles raros, la planta ahora produce el medicamento de forma natural.

**Impacto** – Este avance podría hacer que la producción de paclitaxel sea más rápida, económica y sostenible. También podría ayudar a aumentar el acceso a este medicamento vital para pacientes con cáncer en todo el mundo, especialmente donde los suministros son limitados.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos trabajarán para aumentar la cantidad de medicamento que la planta produce y probarán cómo escalar este método para la fabricación industrial.

**Frase clave** – Una planta relacionada con el tabaco ha sido modificada para producir el medicamento contra el cáncer paclitaxel, ofreciendo una nueva forma de fabricar este medicamento importante de manera más eficiente y sostenible.
